slides.title: EcoSched
bullets: Energy-aware data center scheduling
An isolated placement change reveals an energy/performance trade-off.
AMS 560 Big Data · Stony Brook University
slides.notes: Introduce the team and the central question. We evaluate a specific CPU/memory placement change under shared conditions; we do not claim a universally better scheduler. The final package combines frozen scheduling evidence with a real, separately verified Kafka workload-arrival demonstration. The speaking allocation and suggested timing in these notes are provisional; no course presentation limit was found in the repository.

slides.title: Balanced resources do not automatically mean lower energy
bullets: Consolidation can let idle hosts sleep.
CPU and memory constraints can strand usable capacity.
Balancing more hosts can preserve performance while raising on-time.
slides.notes: Start with the competing mechanisms. Packing can reduce the number of powered servers, while balancing requests can improve feasibility and initial waiting. A machine can be CPU-light yet memory-constrained. Neither balanced occupancy nor a lower migration count is itself an energy objective. Our experiment was designed to retain a negative result if the proposed balance term spreads work too far.

slides.title: Change placement; hold the controller fixed
bullets: Primary pair: CPU LR-MMT ↔ CPU/memory LR-MMT
Same workload, hosts, simulator and SPECpower mapping
Same LR detector, MMT selector, FIFO and migration assumptions
First Fit and Best Fit are additional baselines.
slides.notes: Explain the controlled ablation before showing results. CPU-oriented placement still enforces memory feasibility; only its scoring term omits explicit balance. Both primary variants share one LR/MMT implementation and its settings. The additional baselines do not consolidate, so their comparison is broader than placement alone. No same-job, payback or later controller extension enters the active conclusions.

slides.title: A common feasibility rule; one extra scoring term
bullets: First Fit: powered-host-first feasible host
Best Fit: fullest feasible CPU host, preferring powered hosts
CPU LR-MMT: normalized incremental power
Memory-aware: power score + 0.25 × |CPU − memory|
slides.notes: Both resources must physically fit for every policy, and FIFO admission remains shared. LR uses past/current aggregate reservations; MMT selects the smallest eligible memory request under a common copy-time model. Safe shadow reservations, all-or-nothing evacuations, cooldown and a per-tick budget prevent contradictory plans. This is an online batch-instance adaptation, not an exact CloudSim/PABFD reproduction. The score is a placement heuristic; the engine accounts for actual modeled transitions.

slides.title: SPECpower supplies a surrogate, not Alibaba electricity
bullets: Three curves applied separately; no physical pooling
Interpolate whole-server watts from requested CPU fraction
Integrate watts × event-interval seconds
Positive energy reduction means savings.
slides.notes: Describe the actual SPECpower points and linear interpolation. Active idle and sleeping are different states. The same selected curve is applied to each sampled host without scaling for CPU core count or RAM, so this is a hardware sensitivity model. kWh equals joules divided by 3.6 million. Wh per completed instance uses completed individual instances, never task groups. These curves are not statistical replications.

bullets: 4 approved policies × 3 sizes × 3 power curves
Fresh simulator per case; fixed configurations and inputs
Energy + waiting + hosts + migrations + pressure
Deterministic, overlapping samples: no significance claim.
slides.notes: The full grid has {runs} active outcomes rather than the historical six-policy grid. The nine primary pairs match workload size and power curve exactly. All active runs complete identical offered work without rejected or unfinished instances. Pressure is requested-resource time above a threshold, not measured application SLA failure. We never average P95 quantiles across runs or categories.

slides.title: Memory-aware placement saves energy in {wins}/{pairs} cases
bullets: Largest workload: {penalty_lo:.2f}–{penalty_hi:.2f}% more modeled energy
Positive reduction = savings; negative = penalty
All small cases improve; only medium Huawei improves.
slides.notes: Pause on the negative bars. The proposed rule saves energy in four of nine conditions, but all largest-workload cases are worse by {penalty_lo:.2f}–{penalty_hi:.2f}%. The small medium Huawei gain is not statistically significant evidence because this is a deterministic grid without independent replications. We preserve each curve separately. This editable chart reproduces the Phase 6 R03 values and sign convention.

slides.title: A larger powered footprint buys modest performance gains
bullets: Selected condition: 4,000 groups · HPE curve
Compare energy, mean powered hosts, waiting and pressure
No single objective establishes scheduler superiority.
slides.notes: Use this one matched condition to explain the trade-off. The energy penalty accompanies more mean active hosts, slightly lower mean initial waiting and lower reservation pressure. All values come from the same two original run summaries. Pressure remains a modeled proxy. Peak hosts, migration pause and P95 outcomes are in the report, not hidden. Pareto comparisons are descriptive only within one size/curve and objective pair.

slides.title: Extra busy-host on-time explains the largest-case penalty
bullets: HPE: {hpe_on_share:.2f}% of its own net gap
Huawei: {huawei_on_share:.2f}%; Quanta: {quanta_on_share:.2f}%
Balance can outweigh power preference among already-on hosts.
slides.notes: D5 decomposes each curve’s net candidate-minus-baseline gap. About 88% in the earlier summary is a pooled descriptive ratio of component sums to gap sums; it is not one physical energy experiment. The separate shares are shown here. The proposed rule wakes fewer servers, but spreads work across more already-on hosts. Extra time with work dominates; idle-empty time contributes little, while fewer wakes offset some cost. This is supported mechanism analysis, not universal production causality.

slides.title: Kafka transports arrivals; it does not run the scheduler
slides.notes: Follow validated input, ordered producer, one Kafka partition, validating consumer, SQLite WAL and Streamlit monitoring. The external controller survives browser reruns and navigation. Persist before manual offset commit. Exact duplicates do not inflate unique instances, while conflicts fail verification. The guarantee is at least once with idempotent persistence; no distributed exactly-once or high availability is claimed.

slides.title: The defensible result is an energy/performance trade-off
bullets: {wins}/{pairs} energy wins; no consistent energy improvement
Largest workloads pay {penalty_lo:.2f}–{penalty_hi:.2f}% more energy
Modest performance gains require an explicit energy budget
D6: validated artifacts, recovery, dashboard and real Kafka replay
slides.notes: Conclude with the actual scientific result: balance-aware placement can improve some performance outcomes but can work against consolidation. Negative findings are useful because the ablation and D5 explain why. Future work should freeze settings and test independent windows, calibrate power/migration assumptions and define application-level acceptability. The team’s code ownership is documented separately from imported commit authorship. Invite questions, then use appendices for exact values and provenance.
